card.hook: Picture a pavement in the middle of Queenstown, with people hanging around outside a shopfront like they're waiting for something very important. They are: burgers. This photo is about that street scene, not a grand view.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Shotover Street pavement, out of the doorway, and face Fergburger so the street leads your eye towards the shopfront. Keep the shop name in the frame and leave a little space around it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the shopfront. Switch to 0.5x if the pavement is narrow or you want the whole street, then try 2x for a tighter shot of the sign or the people outside.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the shopfront up on one of the vertical lines so it looks straight.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, so you get a clean shot of the street. Dusk is the other good time, when the signs and shopfronts glow.
card.selfie_here: Head to the stairs directly across Shotover Street from the Fergburger entrance (42 Shotover Street) and stand with the burger shop behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the shopfront over your shoulder. We only have one report of this spot and it doesn't say which way the shop falls in your frame, so check the angle on the spot.
card.rules_and_safety: Fergburger is a working restaurant on a public street, so shoot from the pavement and stay out of the doorway. If you want a close-up of a burger or the bakery counter, ask politely and keep out of other customers' way.
card.challenge: Get the whole shop name in the frame with breathing room around it, plus one hungry-looking person in the queue, and no one gets cropped.
card.good_to_know: Fergburger began in February 2001 in a garage off Cow Lane, where it was hard to find and grew mainly by word of mouth. It now sits on Shotover Street beside its bakery, Ferg Baker, which opened in 2011, and a bar that opened in July 2020. The menu includes lamb, venison, cod, falafel and tofu burgers.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Shotover Street pavement, out of the doorway, and face Fergburger so the street leads your eye towards the shopfront. Keep the shop name in the frame and leave a little space around it.

card.hook: You step out of a cabin on Bob's Peak, about 450 metres above Lake Wakatipu, and the whole town is laid out below you like a model village. Rooftops, lake and mountain ridges all fit in one shot, which is pretty unfair on every other viewpoint.
card.stand_here: Stand at the top viewpoint of the Skyline Queenstown Gondola, right at the phone icon on the map (it shows how far away you are). Face out over the town and Lake Wakatipu.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the big view of town, lake and mountains. Go 0.5x for the gondola cabins and terminal buildings, then zoom 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out Walter Peak, Cecil Peak or The Remarkables.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the distant mountains, then drag the slider to make the picture a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour and detail.
card.best_time: Clear days show the most distant peaks. Late afternoon to evening usually gives softer light on the mountains, and dusk adds the town lights. Check the official site for operating times first.
card.selfie_here: Try the gondola station terrace at the top, which has an unobstructed city view, though it gets busy at sunset. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the town and lake over your shoulder. The framed artwork a short walk from the gondola exit is an easy first selfie before you reach the viewing decks.
card.rules_and_safety: You can't take photos while riding the luge. Handheld cameras, selfie sticks and unsecured devices aren't allowed on the Vortex Slide. Building work is going on at the top, so the artwork and terrace may be affected.
card.challenge: Take one shot of the whole view, then find the single mountain peak you like best and fill the screen with just that.
card.good_to_know: The gondola opened officially on 17 November 1967. The hill was a popular vantage point, but it was hard to reach until a road was cut in 1961. New gondolas and a new base terminal arrived in 2023, and building work at the top was still going on at the time of writing, so things may look different from older photos.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the top viewpoint of the Skyline Queenstown Gondola, right at the phone icon on the map (it shows how far away you are). Face out over the town and Lake Wakatipu.

selfie_spots.why: A travel blog flags this framed artwork near the arrival point as a photo stop, which makes it an easy first selfie before you reach the viewing decks.

card.hook: Walk to the very end of the Queenstown Gardens peninsula and the lake is on several sides of you, with The Remarkables sitting across the water like they know you've got a camera. It's the spot everyone drifts towards, and it's easy to see why.
card.stand_here: Go to the tip of the peninsula in Queenstown Gardens and look south-east towards the subject about 100 m away, facing south across the lake. Lake Wakatipu fills the foreground and The Remarkables ridge rises on the far side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the lake and the ridge together. Switch to 0.5x for more foreground water, or 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the peaks of The Remarkables.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the peaks, then slide it a little darker so the golden light doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset is the one to aim for, when the peaks pick up golden light. Sunny summer days get busy, so go early if you want the paths to yourself.
card.selfie_here: Try the little footbridge across the lily pond: turn on the front camera and stand on the bridge with the pond and gardens behind you (there's a bench close by). At the far tip of the peninsula, turn so the open lake and mountains are behind you, which is a good sunset selfie spot. Try 0.5x to fit more in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the wide dirt track of the lakefront walk from Park Street, with the lake on their left, and to frame you with the gardens' peninsula across the Frankton Arm behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Queenstown Gardens is an open public park, but check the official site before you go in case of events or seasonal changes, such as the winter LUMA festival.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines and take one shot with the lake on the bottom third and one with the mountains on the bottom third. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The first two oaks were planted in 1866, and the gardens opened officially in 1867. The rose garden dates from the 1960s, when 850 bushes were planted. The Scott Memorial from 1913 is also worth a look.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the tip of the peninsula in Queenstown Gardens and look south-east towards the subject about 100 m away, facing south across the lake. Lake Wakatipu fills the foreground and The Remarkables ridge rises on the far side.

selfie_spots.why: The water lilies and trees around the pond make a calm backdrop, and guides single out this bridge for photos.

card.hook: Picture a woolshed on the lake edge, then a gold rush turning it into a pub. That's the corner you're looking at, and the stone-solid hotel with lake and mountains behind it looks great on a phone.
card.stand_here: Stand on the lakefront about 195 m east of the hotel, towards Queenstown Gardens, and turn to face back towards the town. You'll get the hotel frontage with the lake edge in front of it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the hotel, the lake edge and a bit of town. If the building looks small, try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone), or drop to 0.5x for the big lake-and-mountain scene, where the hotel becomes a small part of the picture.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the hotel on one of the vertical lines so it stands up straight, and let the lake edge lead the eye towards it.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, more even light than midday. At dusk, try night mode and hold your phone steady against a railing or your body.
card.selfie_here: Try Queenstown Beach, reached from Marine Parade. A guide calls it a popular photo spot at the water's edge, but nobody has confirmed the hotel shows up behind you, so check your screen. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you can, and step along until the building sits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from public spaces like the lakefront and Marine Parade. If you want to go inside or into the courtyard, check before you go, as it's a private, paid-stay hotel.
card.challenge: Take the same shot twice: once from the lakefront and once from Marine Parade. Then pick the winner, a straight-on close-up or the wide view with the lake out front.
card.good_to_know: William Rees, one of the first European settlers here, had a woolshed on this spot. After gold turned up in the Shotover River in 1862, he turned it into a hotel called the Queen's Arms. Albert Eichardt joined him in 1866 and was sole proprietor by 1869, which is why his name stuck. It's a Category Two historic place, was badly hit by the November 1999 floods, and reopened in December 2001.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the lakefront about 195 m east of the hotel, towards Queenstown Gardens, and turn to face back towards the town. You'll get the hotel frontage with the lake edge in front of it.

card.hook: Picture a vintage steamer tied up at a pier, with a wall of mountains standing right behind her. That's the TSS Earnslaw at Steamer Wharf, and Queenstown hands you the whole scene in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand on Steamer Wharf, on the Queenstown Bay lakefront. Face the ship with the lake in front of you and the Remarkables rising behind her.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the ship with the Remarkables behind. Go 0.5x if you want more wharf and sky, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for a close shot of the funnel and hull.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the ship on one of the side lines and keep the mountains along the top third, with the water line level.
card.best_time: Sunrise is lovely, with the ship docked below the Remarkables. The Earnslaw sails to a schedule, so check her departure times first so you know when she'll be at the wharf or coming round the bay to dock.
card.selfie_here: Try the wharf at the end of Beach Street, beside her berth. Use the front camera at 0.5x and face the town so she's behind you. Nobody's marked this as an official selfie spot, so check the angle when you get there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by at Earnslaw Park on Lower Beech Street, at the water's edge in Queenstown Bay, to take your photo while the ship sits at dock behind you.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one tight shot of the funnel, then see which one makes your friends say 'where's that?'
card.good_to_know: Steamer Wharf is Queenstown's historic lakefront pier, and it's the home berth of the TSS Earnslaw. The wharf is lined with cafés and bars, so you can grab a drink while you wait for the right moment. Snap a few frames in case people walk through.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Steamer Wharf, on the Queenstown Bay lakefront. Face the ship with the lake in front of you and the Remarkables rising behind her.

card.hook: Nearly every photo you'll see of Queenstown Hill is taken from the top. This one flips it: you're snapping the hill itself, and it's worth it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Moonlight Track above Arthurs Point, on the Shotover River side, and face the hill, which is to the south-east. The exact spot isn't fixed, so walk until you find a clear gap in the trees with the whole ridge in view.
card.zoom: Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the ridge, or zoom 1x if you want more of the valley around it. Skip zoom 0.5x here, because it makes the hill look small and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the ridge line on the top third, and tap the hill, then slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright so the trees and tussock keep their colour.
card.best_time: Go early morning or late afternoon, when the lower sun gives the slopes shape and warmer colours. Midday light tends to flatten the hillside.
card.selfie_here: The hill would be under your feet rather than behind you, so for a selfie head up to the Basket of Dreams sculpture on the Queenstown Hill Time Walk, before the summit. Use the front camera and sit in the basket-shaped steel seat, with the Remarkables or Cecil Peak framed through the metalwork.
card.rules_and_safety: Check access and conditions on the ground or with the official track information before you go, as they can change.
card.challenge: Fit all three layers into one shot: houses at the bottom, a band of trees in the middle, bare tussock on top.
card.good_to_know: Queenstown Hill is 907 metres high. Its Māori name, Te Tapu-nui, means 'mountain of intense sacredness'. Houses sit on the lower slopes, wilding conifers like Douglas fir and larch cover the middle, and it's a working sheep farm.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Moonlight Track above Arthurs Point, on the Shotover River side, and face the hill, which is to the south-east. The exact spot isn't fixed, so walk until you find a clear gap in the trees with the whole ridge in view.

None of the pages I found names a spot in town where the hill is the backdrop, so I could not give a passer-by position that frames the whole hill; I left ask_someone_spot null rather than guess. The Time Walk gateway (a metal millennium gate on Belfast Terrace) is named, but no page says it frames the hill. No page states selfie stick or tripod rules. The position given (-45.00867, 168.69242) is about 2 km from the Belfast Terrace trailhead that pages cite (about -45.0275, 168.6666), so check it before using it.

card.hook: You don't have to climb all 1,748 metres of Ben Lomond to get the good photo. Stop at the saddle, turn around, and Lake Wakatipu and Queenstown are laid out below you like a map.
card.stand_here: Stand at Ben Lomond Saddle, on the track between the lower slopes and the summit. Ben Lomond rises north-west of Queenstown town centre, with its summit about 4 km away. Face uphill and the summit climb is straight ahead of you.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the whole slope and sky, then zoom 1x when you turn round for the lake and town. Zoom 2x to 5x, if your phone has it, helps pick out the summit ridge.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the track in the lower third of the frame so it leads the eye up to the summit.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day. Check the track conditions first, because the upper track is often icy in winter.
card.selfie_here: Try the ground behind the Skyline Gondola building on Bob's Peak, where you can see the Ben Lomond summit. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and tuck the summit in behind your shoulder. The viewpoint at the top of Queenstown Hill also works, with Ben Lomond among the peaks behind you.
card.ask_someone: At the first clearing on the track, about 15 minutes up from the top of the Skyline Gondola, the summit first comes into view ahead, so hand your phone to a passing hiker and stand with the summit behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The summit can get very icy and dangerous in winter, so summer is the better time to hike. The saddle is a point on the track, not a signed lookout, so check the trail before you go.
card.challenge: Take two shots from the same spot: one looking up at the summit, one looking back at the lake, then see which one your friends 'like' more.
card.good_to_know: Ben Lomond was named after Ben Lomond in Scotland by an early shepherd, Duncan McAusland. The track climbs through Douglas fir forest, then mountain beech, then opens into tussock grassland. The full summit hike is a 5 to 8 hour return trip, so many visitors stop at the saddle.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Ben Lomond Saddle, on the track between the lower slopes and the summit. Ben Lomond rises north-west of Queenstown town centre, with its summit about 4 km away. Face uphill and the summit climb is straight ahead of you.
